question_text: Examine the need for electoral reforms as suggested by various committees, with particular reference to the "one nation, one election" principle.
topic: Electoral reform and one nation, one election
topics: Electoral reform and one nation, one election
customKeyPointers: Frequent elections keep the government in campaign mode
One cycle would cut cost and a policy freeze, and it would bind unlike mandates together
This form of the reform needs the states' consent

points.text: Electoral reform is needed because money, a criminal candidature and an endless campaign have weakened the poll.
Committees have asked for transparency of funding, a bar on serious crime, and a more stable electoral calendar.
One nation, one election would reduce cost and the pause that a model code imposes, but it would also yoke a state mandate to a national wave.
The need for reform is clear. This one principle should not be passed as if it were the whole of that reform.

question_text: Explain and distinguish between Lok Adalats and Arbitration Tribunals. Do they entertain civil as well as criminal cases?
topic: Lok Adalat and arbitration
topics: Lok Adalat and arbitration
customKeyPointers: A Lok Adalat settles; an arbitrator decides
One is a legal-services forum, the other a private tribunal the parties chose
A non-compoundable criminal case belongs in neither

points.text: A Lok Adalat is a statutory forum that settles a dispute by consent. An arbitration tribunal is a private body the parties appoint to give a binding award.
The Lok Adalat is free, informal and its settlement is a decree. Arbitration is contractual, can be costly, and its award is enforced as a decree unless set aside.
Both deal with civil and commercial matters. A Lok Adalat may also take a compoundable criminal case. A non-compoundable offence is outside both.
They are not two speeds of the same court. One reconciles. The other adjudicates, and neither is a criminal court.

question_text: "The growth of the cabinet system has practically resulted in the marginalisation of parliamentary supremacy." Elucidate.
topic: Cabinet power and parliamentary supremacy
topics: Cabinet power and parliamentary supremacy
customKeyPointers: The Cabinet holds the majority, the timetable and the information
Scrutiny has moved to a committee the House may not read
Supremacy remains the rule if the government loses its majority

points.text: Parliamentary supremacy remains the theory. A disciplined cabinet has become the practice.
The executive draws the bills, controls time, and can treat a majority as a guarantee rather than as a debate to be won.
Questions and committees still exist, but a report the House does not discuss is a weak substitute for supremacy.
The cabinet has marginalised the day-to-day supremacy of Parliament. It has not abolished the fact that it governs only while it holds the House.

question_text: "The duty of the Comptroller and Auditor General is not merely to ensure the legality of expenditure but also its propriety." Comment.
topic: Legality and propriety in the CAG's audit
topics: Legality and propriety in the CAG's audit
customKeyPointers: Legality asks whether the spend was permitted
Propriety asks whether it was wise, fair and in the public interest
The CAG can report a waste that broke no rule

points.text: A legal expenditure can still be an improper one, and the CAG is expected to say so.
Legality is whether the sanction, the rule and the appropriation existed. Propriety is whether the money served a public purpose at a reasonable cost.
An audit that stops at legality would pass a wasteful but authorised scheme. Propriety is why audit reports discuss extravagance, delay and a benefit that never arrived.
The duty is both. Parliament needs to know not only that the spend was allowed, but whether it ought to have been made.

question_text: Analyse the role of local bodies in providing good governance at the local level and bring out the pros and cons of merging the rural local bodies with the urban local bodies.
topic: Local bodies and merging rural with urban
topics: Local bodies and merging rural with urban
customKeyPointers: Rural and urban bodies were separated because their problems differ
A merger can plan a fringe that is no longer only a village
It can also let the town's politics swallow the village's voice

points.text: Local bodies are the level at which water, waste, a street light and a certificate are either governed or neglected.
They work when they have a function, a fund and a functionary. Most still implement a scheme someone else designed.
Merging a rural body into an urban one can coordinate the growing fringe. It can also replace a village priority with a city one, and dilute a reserved voice.
The merger is useful at a real urban edge and harmful as a general rule.

question_text: Public charitable trusts have the potential to make India's development more inclusive as they relate to certain vital public issues. Comment.
topic: Public charitable trusts and inclusive development
topics: Public charitable trusts and inclusive development
customKeyPointers: A trust can hold a school, a hospital or a scholarship outside the annual budget
A weak regulator lets a trust become a private fund with a public name
The potential is real and it is not self-executing

points.text: A public charitable trust can fund a lasting public good that a one-year budget will not protect.
Education, health and relief are the vital issues where a well-run trust has widened access.
The same form can be captured by a family, a political purpose or a tax plan, and then the inclusion is only in the deed.
The potential is genuine where the trust is transparent and aimed at the person the state is missing. It is not automatic.

question_text: Poverty and malnutrition create a vicious cycle, adversely affecting human capital formation. What steps can be taken to break the cycle?
topic: Poverty and malnutrition
topics: Poverty and malnutrition
customKeyPointers: A poor household eats poorly, and a poorly nourished child learns and earns less
The cycle is early: pregnancy, the first two years, then the school
A scheme that reaches the child late has already lost the cycle

points.text: Poverty produces malnutrition, and malnutrition produces a weaker capacity to leave poverty.
The break has to come in pregnancy and the first thousand days: a meal, iron, a vaccination and a check that is actually done.
A school meal, a creche and a wage for the mother keep the older child from becoming the next turn of the same cycle.
Human capital is not formed by a scholarship at eighteen if the body was stunted at two.

question_text: The doctrine of democratic governance makes it necessary that the public perception of the integrity and commitment of civil servants becomes absolutely positive. Discuss.
topic: Public perception of civil servants
topics: Public perception of civil servants
customKeyPointers: Democratic consent runs on a believed integrity
An honest service that is rude, slow or opaque will still be disbelieved
The remedy is conduct a citizen can see, not a slogan

points.text: A democracy cannot long ask people to obey a service they believe is for sale or indifferent.
Integrity has to be visible in a file that moves, a refusal that is recorded, and a punishment that is not only of the junior.
Commitment is perceived in a field visit that changes something, not in a mission statement.
An absolutely positive perception is a high bar. A service that is regularly fair can approach it. One that asks to be trusted on its word cannot.

question_text: 'The West is fostering India as an alternative to reduce dependence on China's supply chain and as a strategic ally to counter China's political and economic dominance.' Explain this statement with examples.
topic: India in Western supply chains and strategy
topics: India in Western supply chains and strategy
subTopics: India as an alternative to China
customKeyPointers: The West wants a second source and a second partner in Asia
Investment and technology are the economic half; the Quad is the strategic half
India is being courted, and it is not agreeing to be enlisted

points.text: Western governments and firms are treating India as a place to make what they no longer want to make only in China, and as a power that shares their worry about Beijing.
The economic examples are a push for electronics and semiconductor assembly, and incentives that favour a shift of supply out of China.
The strategic examples are the Quad, deeper defence cooperation with the United States and France, and a common language on a free Indo-Pacific.
The statement is broadly right. India's own interest is to take the investment without becoming a junior camp.

question_text: Critically analyse India's evolving diplomatic, economic and strategic relations with the Central Asian Republics (CARs), highlighting their increasing significance in regional and global geopolitics.
topic: India and the Central Asian republics
topics: India and the Central Asian republics
customKeyPointers: Central Asia sits on energy, a corridor and a security problem
The relationship has grown in summits and remained thin on the ground
The land route runs through difficult neighbours

points.text: The Central Asian republics matter more, and India's relations with them are deeper on paper than on the map.
Diplomacy has a regular summit format. Energy, uranium and a small trade are the economic content. Security cooperation against terror is the strategic content.
Their significance is the overlap of Eurasian corridors, a Russian retreat and a Chinese arrival. India wants to be present in that overlap.
The evolution is real and still blocked by geography. Without a reliable route, the relationship stays a dialogue.

question_text: What are the aims and objects of the recently passed and enforced Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024? Are University and State Education Board examinations also covered under the Act?
topic: The Public Examinations Act, 2024
topics: The Public Examinations Act, 2024
customKeyPointers: The Act aims at organised cheating, not one candidate's slip
It targets paper leaks, solver gangs and a colluding official
University and most State Board exams are outside its present list

points.text: The 2024 Act was passed to treat a paper leak as an organised offence against a public examination, not as a mere malpractice.
Its objects are to deter leakage, impersonation and a tampering of the process, and to punish a service provider and an official who collude, with a stiff fine and imprisonment.
It covers examinations conducted by notified public authorities such as the Union's recruitment and higher-education testing bodies.
A university examination and a State Education Board examination are not automatically covered, unless they are brought in by notification or a corresponding state law.
The aim is to make the leak unprofitable. The coverage is of specified public examinations, not of every exam in the country.

question_text: Right to privacy is intrinsic to life and personal liberty and is inherently protected under Article 21 of the Constitution. Explain. In this reference discuss the law relating to DNA testing of a child in the womb to establish its paternity.
topic: Privacy, Article 21 and prenatal DNA testing
topics: Privacy, Article 21 and prenatal DNA testing
subTopics: Privacy and a prenatal DNA test
customKeyPointers: Privacy was read into Article 21 as part of dignity and liberty
It can still be limited by a fair law
A DNA test of a foetus is allowed only for a compelling need, not for curiosity

points.text: After Puttaswamy, privacy is not a privilege granted by statute. It is part of life and personal liberty under Article 21.
The court held it inherent in dignity, autonomy and the right to be left alone, subject to a law that is fair, necessary and proportionate.
A DNA test of a child in the womb takes bodily material and creates information about parentage that cannot be unlearned. It engages the privacy of the woman and of the future child.

Courts allow such a test only where paternity cannot otherwise be fairly decided and the need outweighs the intrusion, with consent and a safeguard on the data. It is not a routine step in every dispute.
Article 21 protects the privacy. A prenatal test is lawful only as a narrow exception, not as a right of anyone who wants to know.

question_text: What changes has the Union Government recently introduced in the domain of Centre-State relations? Suggest measures to build trust between the Centre and the States and to strengthen federalism.
topic: Recent Centre-State changes and trust
topics: Recent Centre-State changes and trust
customKeyPointers: Recent years brought a fiscal rearrangement and a more central use of agencies
Trust falls when a state learns late of a decision that concerns it
The remedy is consultation, a predictable transfer and respect for the State List

points.text: Centre-State relations have been rearranged by a goods and services tax, a greater use of central schemes, and a more active role for central agencies in the states.
Some of this is coordination. Some of it is felt by states as a shrinking of their fiscal and administrative room, especially when dues or a discretion arrive late.
Trust is built by a regular forum that meets, by sharing a draft before it becomes a law, and by a transfer that a state can budget on.
Federalism is strengthened when a governor, an agency and a scheme operate inside their reasons, and when a dispute has a fast, accepted way to be heard.
The recent direction has been toward the Union. The corrective is not a weaker Centre. It is a Centre that does not surprise the states.

question_text: Explain the reasons for the growth of public interest litigation in India. As a result, has the Indian Supreme Court emerged as the world's most powerful judiciary?
topic: Public interest litigation and judicial power
topics: Public interest litigation and judicial power
customKeyPointers: PIL grew because a rights gap and a willing court met
The court then entered policy the executive had left undone
Powerful, yes; the most powerful in the world is a claim, not a finding

points.text: Public interest litigation grew because the people most in need of a right were the least able to file a traditional case.
A relaxed locus, an epistle treated as a petition, and judges willing to monitor a government failure turned the Supreme Court into a forum for prisons, the environment and a bonded labour.
That role expanded further whenever the legislature and the executive left a vacuum.

The court is among the most interventionist in the world. Calling it simply the most powerful ignores courts elsewhere with a strike-down power, and it ignores the fact that Indian judgments still depend on an executive to be obeyed.
PIL made the Court far more powerful. 'The most powerful' is a flourish, not a measured conclusion.

question_text: Discuss India as a secular state and compare it with the secular principles of the US Constitution.
topic: Indian and American secularism
topics: Indian and American secularism
customKeyPointers: India keeps a distance and may still reform a religion
The United States builds a wall that stops both help and hindrance
Both forbid a theocratic state, and they do not forbid it in the same way

points.text: India is a secular state that engages with religion. The United States is a secular state that tries not to.

The Indian Constitution has no established church, guarantees freedom of religion, and also lets the state regulate a secular practice and open a temple. It expressly allows certain protections for minorities.
The American First Amendment stops Congress from establishing a religion or prohibiting its free exercise, and the court has read this as a wall against endorsement and against most public aid.
India will fund a school of a minority and reform a personal law. The American principle is more suspicious of both.
Both are secular. India's secularism is a reformist equidistance. America's is a separation.

question_text: The Citizens' Charter has been a landmark initiative in ensuring citizen-centric administration. But it is yet to reach its full potential. Identify the factors hindering the realisation of its promise and suggest measures to overcome them.
topic: Why the Citizens' Charter underperforms
topics: Why the Citizens' Charter underperforms
customKeyPointers: The charter promised a standard, a time and a remedy
It was often a poster, without the citizen or a penalty
It works when a missed deadline has a consequence

points.text: The Citizens' Charter was meant to turn a department's duty into a standard a citizen could quote.
Many charters were written inside the office, copied from another office, and never revised. They named no officer and no compensation.
A shortage of staff, no link to the grievance system, and a public that does not know the charter exist, stopped the promise.
The measures are to draft it with users, to publish a real timeline, to name the person, and to attach a compensation and a review when the timeline is missed.
A charter without a consequence is a brochure. The potential is the consequence.

question_text: In a crucial domain like the public healthcare system, the Indian state should play a vital role to contain the adverse impact of marketisation of the system. Suggest measures through which the state can enhance the reach of public healthcare at the grassroots level.
topic: Public healthcare against marketisation
topics: Public healthcare against marketisation
customKeyPointers: A market in health serves the person who can pay
Reach at the grassroots is a staffed centre, a drug and a referral that works
Insurance that only pays a private bed is not that reach

points.text: Marketisation of healthcare raises cost and leaves the person who cannot pay outside. The state has to hold the floor.
A staffed sub-centre and primary centre, with medicines in stock and a nurse who is actually posted, is the first measure.
A reliable referral, a free essential drug, and a community health worker who is paid and trusted extend that reach into the hamlet.
Regulation of private prices and a public option that is good enough to use contain the market without pretending it will vanish.
The state enhances reach by being present at the bottom, not only by paying a bill at the top.

question_text: e-governance is not just about the routine application of digital technology in service delivery. It is as much about multifarious interactions for ensuring transparency and accountability. In this context evaluate the role of the 'interactive service model' of e-governance.
topic: The interactive service model of e-governance
topics: The interactive service model of e-governance
keyPointers: Transparency and the right to information
customKeyPointers: A routine portal delivers a service one way
An interactive model lets the citizen ask, complain and see the answer
It fails when the interaction is a form that nobody reads

points.text: The interactive service model treats e-governance as a conversation, not as a form the office pushes out.
The citizen can apply, track, object and rate, and the department is supposed to answer inside the same system.
That interaction is what turns a digital service into transparency, because the status is visible, and into accountability, because a delay has a name.
In practice many systems stop at the application. The reply is late, the grievance is closed without a reason, and the interaction is only technical.
The model is the right idea. It works only where an officer is bound to answer inside it.

question_text: 'Terrorism has become a significant threat to global peace and security.' Evaluate the effectiveness of the United Nations Security Council's Counter-Terrorism Committee (CTC) and its associated bodies in addressing and mitigating this threat at the international level.
topic: The UN Counter-Terrorism Committee
topics: The UN Counter-Terrorism Committee
customKeyPointers: The Counter-Terrorism Committee set a common standard after 2001
It can monitor and embarrass, and it cannot compel a divided Council
The effect is real on norms and limited on a state that will not act

points.text: The Counter-Terrorism Committee was the Security Council's answer to a threat that no one state could police alone.
It pressed states to criminalise terror financing, to share information and to report. Its executive directorate visits and advises.
Associated bodies, including the sanctions machinery, can list a person and a fund, and can help a weaker state write a law.
The limit is political. A permanent member's interest, a dispute over who is a terrorist, and the absence of a standing force mean the committee mitigates more than it ends.
It has been effective as a standard-setter and a helper. It has not been effective as a decider the great powers must obey.

question_text: Discuss the geopolitical and geostrategic importance of Maldives for India, with a focus on global trade and energy flows. Further, discuss how this relationship affects India's maritime security and regional stability amidst international competition.
topic: Maldives, trade flows and India's maritime security
topics: Maldives, trade flows and India's maritime security
customKeyPointers: Maldives sits on the sea lane that carries India's trade and energy
A friendly Male is an outer watch on the Indian Ocean
A hostile or heavily indebted Male is a rival's opening

points.text: The Maldives matters to India because it sits astride the lanes by which the Indian Ocean's trade and energy move.
A large share of India's cargo and fuel passes near these islands. A cooperative Maldives is an early warning and a partner in surveillance.
The same location draws other powers. A base, a port deal or a political swing in Male changes India's security more than the islands' size suggests.
Regional stability depends on the Maldives not becoming a stage for that competition, and on India being a steady partner rather than an overbearing one.
The relationship is geostrategic. It protects a flow of trade and energy by keeping a small state from becoming someone else's foothold.
